newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish envoy to Cuba cautions his government.
newsitem.headline: Spanish envoy to Cuba cautions his government.

text.p: Spain's outgoing ambassador to Cuba suggested in an interview published on Sunday that his country was at risk of losing influence in Latin America.

Ambassador Edualdo Mirapeix left his post on Thursday amid a bitter diplomatic row between Madrid and Havana over demands by Spain's seven-month-old conservative government for democratic reform in Cuba. His departure was planned before the dispute.

"In these years, Spain's ability to influence Cuba is being risked, not only the ability to have a presence on the island but also in other areas of Latin American," Mirapeix told the Spanish daily El Pais.
Last month Cuba withdrew its earlier approval for a new Spanish ambassador, Jose Coderch, in protest against what it called Spanish interference in its affairs.
The withdrawal followed efforts by Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government to spearhead a toughening of European Union policy on Cuba.
Spain says it could take months to name another ambassador.
The government had chosen Coderch to replace Mirapeix, who the former Socialist government appointed, to demonstrate its shift to a tougher line against the one-party communist government in Havana.
Mirapeix echoed a warning by Felipe Gonzalez, the Socialist opposition leader and former prime minister, that other nations would seek to fill any vaccum in Spanish-Cuban economic ties.

"There are many countries in Europe and outside of it which are very attentive to the possibilities the Cuban market can offer in the future and who are going to take advantage of any space to access it," the former ambassador said.
He said it would be a mistake to say there have not been changes in Cuba in recent years.

He rejected measures such as the U.S. economic blockade of Cuba which he said could have the "boomerang effect" of pushing the Havana government towards a more closed policy rather than an opening up to democracy.
He said the Aznar government and its Socialist predecessor shared the same objectives in Cuba and only differed in "where they put the accent".
